name: The Model Judge
oneLiner: Benchmarks multiple LLMs on one shared prompt set, scores each answer with an LLM-as-judge rubric, and ranks them to name a winner.
lead: Any assistant can be backed by several candidate models, and they don't score equally. This agent runs one fixed prompt set through each model, scores every response on a shared rubric, and lays the results side by side so the model choice rests on evidence, not preference.
chore: Benchmarking models by hand means opening each one, pasting the same prompt, copying the answer into a spreadsheet, and repeating that across dozens of prompts and five or six models — then eyeballing accuracy, clarity, and hallucination with no consistent scale. It takes days, and one tired reviewer is not a reproducible scoreboard.
instead: Every model answers every prompt automatically, each response is scored on the same rubric, and you get a ranked scoreboard with a named winner, a pass rate, and a recommendation — in one run.
whyItMatters: The backing model decides whether the assistant ships accurate answers or confident hallucinations, so the choice needs a benchmark, not a hunch.

howItWorks.step: Resolves the model set to benchmark: named in-house models from `APP_MODELS`, a default pair when none are named, plus enabled `EXTERNAL_MODELS` (Gemini, Claude) when `--include-external` is set. Throws below two.
howItWorks.explain: Resolution is **precedence-ordered**: an explicitly requested id is looked up in `APP_MODELS` first and only falls through to `EXTERNAL_MODELS` if it isn't an in-house model — and an external match is dropped unless `external.enabled`, so a disabled provider never enters the run. With no `input.models` it defaults to the `gpt4o`/`gpt4omini` pair; `--include-external` then appends every external that is enabled, not `onDemand`, and not already present (the dedupe guard stops a requested id being added twice). The real guard is **`models.length < 2`**: a comparison needs at least two contestants, so a typo'd single id or an all-disabled external set fails fast instead of producing a meaningless one-model ranking.

howItWorks.step: Sends the identical prompt to each model and captures the response text plus latency, before any scoring runs.
howItWorks.explain: Provider-routed dispatch: `provider === 'app'` goes through the in-house chat client with a generous `timeout: 180000` (3 min) — a cold model shouldn't false-fail on latency alone, since a premature timeout would register as a failed answer rather than a slow one. The key design choice is that **latency is captured as a first-class result** (`responseTimeMs`) right beside the answer text and before any scoring runs, so a model that scores well but answers slowly stays visible in the ranking. The `gemini` and `claude` branches hit their own direct-API helpers that return the same `{answer, timeMs}` shape, keeping downstream scoring provider-agnostic; only these three providers ever arrive here because `resolveModels` already filtered the set.

howItWorks.step: Scores each response with an LLM-as-judge (`gpt4omini`) on six rubric dimensions, 1-10 each, returned as strict JSON.
howItWorks.explain: This is the **LLM-as-judge** core: `gpt4omini` scores the answer 1-10 on six dimensions, and the prompt hard-requires JSON-only output so the reply can be parsed. `judgeAnswer.match(/\{[^}]+\}/)` extracts the first `{...}` block — a defensive guard against a judge that wraps its JSON in prose despite the instruction (a common LLM quirk), safe only because the flat rubric object has no nested braces for the non-greedy `[^}]+` to trip on. Each raw score is **clamped to 1-10** with `|| 5` filling any missing dimension with a neutral value, so a partial judge reply degrades rather than crashes; scores normalize to 0-1 and each is gated at `>= 0.70` — meaning `passed` is per-dimension, while `averageNormalized` is the single aggregate the ranking ultimately sorts on.

howItWorks.step: After the full matrix runs, aggregates per model: mean aggregate score, PASS count, pass rate, and mean latency.
howItWorks.explain: Per-model roll-up over the full matrix, where the **`!r.error` filter is load-bearing**: errored responses are excluded from every average, so a model that timed out on three prompts isn't dragged down by counting those as zeros — they simply don't count toward `total`. `passCount` tallies the `verdict === 'PASS'` field (not the raw score), and both `avgAggregate` and `avgResponseTimeMs` are guarded by `total > 0` to dodge a divide-by-zero when every prompt for a model errored. `passRate` is rendered as a rounded percentage **string** (`'82%'`) purely for display, while `avgAggregate` stays a 3-decimal number — the ranking sorts on the number, never the string.

howItWorks.step: Ranks models by mean aggregate, names a winner, and writes a recommendation calibrated by the top-to-bottom score gap (< 0.05 is a tie, decide on latency and cost).
howItWorks.explain: The recommendation is calibrated by the **score gap**, not the raw winner: `sorted` arrives ranked by `avgAggregate` descending, so `sorted[0]` is best and `sorted[sorted.length - 1]` worst, and the gap between them is bucketed — **`< 0.05`** means effectively tied, flipping the advice to 'choose on latency and cost'; **`< 0.15`** is a moderate trade-off; anything larger is a clear win worth acting on. These thresholds exist because a rubric-scored aggregate carries noise, so a 0.02 lead is not a real difference. It then re-sorts a **copy** (`[...sorted]`) by `avgResponseTimeMs` and, if the fastest model isn't the winner, appends that fact — deliberately surfacing the quality-vs-speed tension rather than hiding it behind the top score.

examples.caption: Two in-house models, head to head
examples.input: A 40-prompt support dataset and two in-house models, `Brain-Fast` and `Brain-Deep`.
examples.output: Scoreboard: Brain-Deep wins at `0.87` aggregate and an 82% pass rate versus Brain-Fast's `0.79`. Gap > 0.15, so the recommendation reads 'Significant gap — strongly recommend Brain-Deep,' with a per-prompt score sheet attached.

examples.caption: Adding external models as a benchmark
examples.input: The same 40 prompts with `--include-external`, benchmarking the in-house model against two well-known external ones.
examples.output: A three-way ranking where the in-house model lands second, 0.03 behind the leader. Gap < 0.05 triggers 'Models perform similarly — choose based on latency and cost,' and the in-house model is flagged fastest at 2,100ms avg.

examples.caption: A `--limit 5` pipeline smoke test
examples.input: First 5 prompts across three models to validate wiring before a full run.
examples.output: A fast mini-report confirming all three models answered, with early scores and latencies, so the dataset, API reachability, and scoring service are all verified before committing to the full 40-prompt run.

underHood.heading: Resolves the model set
underHood.whenRuns: First, before any prompt is sent.
underHood.input: Requested model ids, plus the `--include-external` flag.
underHood.output: A validated `ModelDef[]` of at least two models — in-house registry entries plus enabled external ones (Gemini, Claude) when requested.

underHood.heading: Runs the prompt matrix
underHood.input: One shared prompt from the dataset.
underHood.output: Response text and latency from each model, via the in-house `app` client or the external provider APIs.

underHood.heading: Dual-scores each response
underHood.output: A privacy/safety gate result from the checker service, plus a 1-10 six-dimension rubric score from the LLM-as-judge.

underHood.heading: Combines into a verdict
underHood.input: The gate result and the six rubric scores.
underHood.output: One aggregate score and a PASS / WARNING / FAIL verdict for that response.

underHood.heading: Aggregates the scoreboard
underHood.input: Every scored response across all models.
underHood.output: Per-model means, a ranking, and a gap-calibrated recommendation naming the winner.

underHood.heading: Writes the artifacts
underHood.whenRuns: Last, once the scoreboard is final.
underHood.output: A multi-sheet `.xlsx`, a `.json` data file, and an optional `.docx` cover report.

prerequisites: Node >= 18 and a terminal (macOS/Linux shell or Windows PowerShell).
The assistant API's base URL and access token, so the agent can issue real prompts.
A golden dataset JSON — the file The Answer Grader's convert step emits, or any dataset in that shape.
The toolkit's local scoring service running, so each response gets a privacy/safety and quality check.
(Optional) `GOOGLE_API_KEY` and/or `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` to enable Gemini and Claude as external benchmarks.

steps.label: Install Node.js — the runtime for the agent.
steps.cmd:
# macOS (with Homebrew):
brew install node

# or download the LTS installer from nodejs.org, then check it worked:
node -v   # should print v18 or higher
steps.why: The agent is a TypeScript program executed by Node. One-time install per machine.
steps.firstRun: Needed only the first time on a new machine.

steps.label: Clone the agent code, install dependencies, and start the local scoring service.
steps.cmd:
cd path/to/the-agents
npm install

# one-time: install the scoring service's own dependencies
npm run eval:service:install

# then start it (leave this running in its own terminal tab)
npm run eval:service:start
steps.why: `npm install` pulls the xlsx writer and the model clients. The scoring service is a separate process that runs the privacy/safety and quality checks — it must be listening before a comparison runs.
steps.firstRun: Installs everything and starts the service listening locally.
steps.rerun: Leave the service up across comparisons — no restart needed per run.

steps.label: Point it at the assistant and, optionally, enable external benchmarks (env vars).
steps.cmd:
export APP_API_URL=https://your-assistant-host.example.com
export APP_API_TOKEN=your-access-token
export APP_MODEL=gpt4o
export GOOGLE_API_KEY=your-gemini-key       # optional — enables Gemini as a benchmark
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=your-claude-key    # optional — enables Claude as a benchmark
steps.why: Read at startup: which assistant to call, the token that authorizes it, and which external providers are available. Nothing is hard-coded — swap these to retarget environments.

steps.label: Run a `--limit 5` smoke test, then the full comparison.
steps.cmd:
# quick check — 5 questions, no outside brains, to confirm the pipeline works
npm run eval:compare -- --limit 5

# full run — the assistant's own brains plus Gemini and Claude as benchmarks
npm run eval:compare -- --include-external
steps.why: The limited run verifies the wiring — dataset found, assistant reachable, scoring service up — before spending time and API cost on the full set. `--include-external` adds Gemini and Claude to the matrix.
steps.firstRun: Runs the full prompt matrix, dual-scores each response, and ranks the models.
steps.rerun: Every run is independent — nothing carries over. Re-run any time you need a current scoreboard, e.g. after a model upgrade.

steps.label: Open the scoreboard.
steps.cmd:
open outputs/eval/comparisons/model-comparison-<timestamp>.xlsx
# and the same data as JSON, for feeding into another tool:
open outputs/eval/comparisons/model-comparison-<timestamp>.json
steps.why: The `.xlsx` is the shareable artifact — Model Summary, per-prompt comparison, raw scores, and a latency sheet. The `.json` is the same data for programmatic consumption.

inputs.name: --models <list>
inputs.desc: Comma-separated in-house model ids to include (default: the standard `gpt4o`/`gpt4omini` pair).

inputs.name: --include-external
inputs.desc: Adds enabled external models (Gemini, and Claude when requested by id) as benchmarks.

inputs.name: --limit <n>
inputs.desc: Run only the first N prompts — a smoke test.

inputs.name: --dataset <path>
inputs.desc: Which golden dataset to use; without it, the agent auto-selects the most recently generated one.

outputs.name: model-comparison-<timestamp>.xlsx
outputs.desc: A multi-sheet scoreboard — model summary, per-prompt comparison, raw dimension scores, and latencies.

outputs.name: model-comparison-<timestamp>.docx (optional)
outputs.desc: A cover-page report naming the winner, for sharing outside the team.

runbook.rerun: No incremental mode — every run is a fresh, timestamped comparison. Re-run whenever you need a current scoreboard, e.g. right after a model upgrade or when a new external model becomes available.
runbook.integrate: The winner and recommendation are the evidence for choosing the backing model. Wire a nightly `--limit 5 --include-external` run into CI as a lightweight regression check that the chosen model hasn't silently degraded.

video.caption: 3-4 min screencast: run a head-to-head model comparison and watch the ranked scoreboard build.
script: Open a terminal beside the outputs folder so viewers see both.
Say: 'This agent asks several AI brains the exact same questions, then scores and ranks their answers. Watch.'
Run `node -v` to confirm Node is installed; say one line about what Node is.
Run `npm install` and start the local scoring service; explain it's the thing that grades each answer.
Show the three `export` lines; say 'this is the only place the assistant-specific stuff lives — swap these and it points anywhere.'
Run the quick 5-question check first; narrate the log lines as each brain answers each question.
Run the full comparison with `--include-external`; point out the pause between calls that avoids rate limits.
Open the produced `.xlsx`; scroll to the Model Summary sheet and read out the winner and the pass rates.
Open the Prompt Comparison sheet; show one question where the two brains clearly disagreed.
Close: 'The recommendation line at the bottom is what tells you whether the gap is worth acting on.'
